paragraphs: Once there was a wizard who took the form of a poor man, went from house to house begging, and captured pretty girls. No one knew where he took them, because they were never seen again. One day he came to the door of a man with three pretty daughters. He looked like a weak, poor beggar and carried a basket on his back, as if to collect charitable gifts. He begged for a little food. When the eldest daughter came out and reached towards him with a piece of bread, he merely touched her, and she was forced to jump into his basket. He hurried away in long strides, carrying her to his house in the middle of a dark forest. Everything inside was magnificent. He gave her anything she could wish for and said, “My darling, you will certainly be happy with me. You have everything your heart could desire.” This went on for a few days. Then he said, “I must go on a journey and leave you alone for a short time. Here are the keys to the house. You may go anywhere and look at everything except one room, which this little key opens. I forbid you to enter it on pain of death.” He also gave her an egg. “Keep this egg safe for me,” he said, “and carry it with you all the time. Losing it would bring a great misfortune.”

She took the keys and egg and promised to obey him in everything. Once he had gone, she explored the whole house, from bottom to top, examining everything. The rooms shone with silver and gold. She thought she had never seen such splendour. At last she reached the forbidden door. She wanted to pass by, but her curiosity gave her no peace. She examined the key. It looked like any other. She put it in the keyhole, turned it a little, and the door sprang open. But what did she see inside? In the middle of the room stood a great bloody basin containing human bodies, dead and cut to pieces. Nearby was a wooden block with a gleaming axe on it. She was so terrified that the egg fell from her hand into the basin. She fished it out and tried to wash off the blood, but in vain. It reappeared at once. She washed and scrubbed, but could not get it off.

Before long, the man returned from his journey. The first things he asked for were the key and the egg. She handed them over, trembling. The red spots told him at once that she had entered the bloody room. “Since you went into that room against my wishes,” he said, “you shall return to it against your own. Your life is over.” He threw her down, dragged her there by her hair, cut off her head on the block, and chopped her into pieces until her blood ran over the floor. Then he threw her into the basin with the others.

“Now I will fetch the second one,” the wizard said. Again he took the form of a poor man and went begging at the house. The second daughter brought him bread. As before, he caught her with a touch and carried her away. She fared no better than her sister. Her curiosity led her to open the bloody room and look inside. When the wizard returned, she paid for it with her life. Then he went and brought the third sister, but she was clever and cunning. After he gave her the keys and the egg and left, she first put the egg away very carefully. Then she explored the house and finally entered the forbidden room. Oh, what did she see! Both her sisters lay in the basin, cruelly murdered and cut into pieces. But she began gathering their body parts and putting them in order: heads, bodies, arms and legs. Once nothing was missing, the parts began to move and join themselves together. Both girls opened their eyes and were alive again. They rejoiced, kissed and embraced each other.

When the man returned, he immediately demanded the keys and egg. Seeing no trace of blood, he said, “You have passed the test. You shall be my bride.” Now he had no power over her and had to do whatever she wanted. “Oh, very well,” she said. “First you must take a basketful of gold to my father and mother, carrying it on your own back. Meanwhile, I will prepare the wedding.” She ran to her sisters, whom she had hidden in a small room. “Now I can save you,” she said. “The wretch himself will carry you home. But as soon as you arrive, send help for me.” She put both sisters into a basket and covered them completely with gold, so that no part of them showed. Then she called the wizard. “Carry this basket away now,” she said. “But I will watch from my little window to see whether you stop or rest along the way.”

The wizard lifted the basket onto his back and set off. It weighed him down so heavily that sweat streamed from his face. He sat down, intending to rest, but at once one of the girls inside called, “I’m looking through my little window, and I can see you resting. Go on at once!” He thought his bride was calling and got to his feet again. Once more he was about to sit down when the girl cried, “I’m looking through my little window, and I can see you resting. Go on immediately!” Whenever he stopped, she called this out, forcing him onwards. At last, groaning and breathless, he carried the basket of gold and the two girls into their parents’ house. Meanwhile, back at his home, the bride prepared the wedding feast and invited the wizard’s friends. Then she took a skull with grinning teeth, decorated it with ornaments and a wreath of flowers, carried it to the attic window, and set it there looking out. When everything was ready, she climbed into a barrel of honey. Then she cut open the feather mattress and rolled in its feathers until she looked like a marvellous bird, and no one could recognise her. She left the house. On her way, she met some wedding guests, who asked:

“Oh, Fitcher’s bird, how have you come here?”
“I come from Fitcher’s house quite near.”
“And what is the young bride doing?”
“She has swept everything clean from cellar to attic,
And now she is peeping from the window, I believe.”
At last she met the bridegroom, slowly making his way back. Like the others, he asked:

“Oh, Fitcher’s bird, how have you come here?”
“I come from Fitcher’s house quite near.”
“And what is the young bride doing?”
“She has swept everything clean from cellar to attic,
And now she is peeping from the window, I believe.”

The bridegroom looked up, saw the decorated skull, mistook it for his bride, and nodded a friendly greeting. But once he and all his guests were inside, the bride’s brothers and relatives, sent to rescue her, arrived. They locked every door so no one could escape and set fire to the house. The wizard and all his gang burned.
